title: Habitats: why a frog lives in a pond and moss grows on a wet wall

summary.text: Why does green moss grow on an old brick wall, but not on the shiny granite steps beside it? A habitat is the place where a plant or an animal lives and finds what they need: water, food, air, shelter and the right warmth. A pond, a forest, a desert and the seashore are habitats, and each one suits different living beings. Rocks are part of every habitat. They give shelter, some of them hold water, and over a very long time they crumble into soil. Your child stands a clay diya and a smooth stone in water, puts mustard seeds on top of both, and finds out which one can be a home for a seed.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left an old brick wall with green moss and a small fern; on the right shiny granite steps, bare and dry; a girl looking from one to the other.

intro.hook: Imagine a fish in the hot sand of the Thar desert, and a camel standing in the sea. Why would neither of them be all right for long?
intro.text: The fish needs water all around, to breathe through gills. The camel needs dry land to walk on and fresh water to drink, and the sea is salty. Each living being has a place that suits their body. That place is called their habitat. In this unit we look at habitats near and far: a pond, a forest, a desert, the seashore, and even a rock. Then we test whether a stone can be a home for a seed.
intro.art: A funny picture of a fish flapping on desert sand and a camel standing up to the knees in sea waves, both looking puzzled.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a habitat is, and name what a habitat gives: water, food, air, shelter and the right warmth.
By the end I can name a few habitats, such as a pond, a forest, a desert and the seashore, and one plant and one animal who live in each.
By the end I can say why a plant or an animal does well in one habitat and not in another.
By the end I can say how rocks are part of a habitat: they give shelter, some hold water, and they slowly crumble into soil.
By the end I can guess, test and say what I saw in the diya and stone test.
By the end I can look at living beings in their habitats gently, and leave their homes as I found them.

terms.meaning: A habitat is the place where a plant or an animal lives. It gives them what they need: water, food, air, shelter and the right warmth.
terms.example: A pond is a habitat for frogs and lotus. A forest is a habitat for monkeys and tall trees.
terms.art: Four small pictures: a pond with a frog and lotus, a forest with a monkey, a desert with a camel, and a seashore with a crab.

terms.meaning: A shelter is a place that keeps a living being safe from the hot sun, the rain, the cold or animals that hunt them.
terms.example: A gap between two rocks is a shelter for a lizard. A nest in a tree is a shelter for a baby bird.
terms.art: A lizard peeping out from a gap between two rocks in bright sun.

terms.meaning: A desert is a very dry place, where rain falls only a little in a whole year.
terms.example: The Thar desert in Rajasthan is a habitat for camels and the khejri tree.
terms.art: Sand dunes with a camel and a thorny khejri tree under a hot sun.

terms.meaning: A forest is a place with many trees growing close together.
terms.example: The forests of the Western Ghats are a habitat for lion-tailed macaques and hornbills.
terms.art: A thick green forest with a lion-tailed macaque on a branch and a hornbill flying past.

terms.meaning: Rock is the hard, natural material that the land is made of, deep down. Stones and pebbles are small pieces of rock.
terms.example: Granite is a rock. Many kitchen counters and temple steps are made of granite.
terms.art: A big grey granite boulder with a few small pebbles beside it.

terms.meaning: Soil is the loose top layer of the ground. It is made of tiny bits of rock mixed with bits of dead plants and animals.
terms.example: The soil in a flowerpot holds water for the plant's roots.
terms.art: A hand holding brown soil, with a magnified circle showing tiny rock grains and bits of old leaf.

terms.meaning: Moss is a small, soft green plant that grows in damp places, often on walls, stones and tree bark.
terms.example: In the Kerala monsoon, green moss covers many old compound walls.
terms.art: A close-up of soft green moss on a wet brick wall, with raindrops.

explanations.definition: A habitat is the place where a plant or an animal lives and finds what they need to stay alive: water, food, air, shelter and the right warmth.
explanations.description: Every living being needs water, food and air. They need shelter from the sun, the rain and danger, and the right warmth, not too hot and not too cold. A habitat is a place that gives them all of these. Humans are animals too, and our home and town are our habitat.
examples: A pond gives a frog water for her eggs, insects to eat and mud to hide in.
A tall tree gives a crow a high, safe place for a nest.
Your home gives you water, food, a roof and a safe place to sleep.
explanations.context: This card says what a habitat is and what it gives.
explanations.art: A frog in a pond with labels pointing to the water, an insect, the mud and the shade of a lotus leaf.

explanations.definition: Each habitat has its own water, warmth, food and shelter, so each one suits different plants and animals.
explanations.description: A pond is wet all the time, so fish, frogs and lotus live there. A forest is shady and damp, so monkeys, hornbills and ferns live there. A desert is hot and dry by day, so camels, desert foxes and thorny plants live there. The seashore is sandy and salty, so crabs and coconut palms live there.
examples: Fish breathe with gills, which work only in water.
A camel can go for many days without drinking water.
In the Sundarbans of West Bengal, mangrove trees grow in salty mud where the sea comes in twice a day.
explanations.context: This card says why different habitats have different plants and animals.
explanations.art: Four panels: a pond with fish and a frog, a forest with a hornbill, a desert with a camel, and a seashore with a crab and a coconut palm.

explanations.definition: Plants grow in almost every habitat on land and in water, and each kind of plant grows best in the habitat that suits them.
explanations.description: A lotus grows in a pond. Their roots hold the mud at the bottom, and their wide leaves float on top. A cactus grows in dry, sandy places and stores water in the thick stem. Moss grows on damp walls and stones, and drinks water through their leaves. Plants do not walk, so they live where their seed landed and found what they needed.
examples: A money plant can grow in a bottle of water on a windowsill.
Aloe vera grows well in a sunny pot that dries out between waterings.
Ferns and moss grow on the shady, wet walls of old wells.
explanations.context: This card says how plants grow in different habitats.
explanations.art: A lotus in a pond, a cactus in sand, moss on a wet wall, and a coconut palm on a beach, side by side.

explanations.definition: Animals live in habitats that give them their food, water and shelter, and their bodies suit those places.
explanations.description: A crab on the seashore digs a hole in the wet sand and hides there when the waves come. A squirrel climbs fast and keeps her nest high in a tree, away from cats. A rock agama, a kind of lizard, lies on a warm rock in the morning sun, and he hides in a crack when danger comes. Animals can move, so they can go and look for a better place when their habitat changes.
examples: Ghost crabs run across the beach at Marina in Chennai and dive into their holes.
Rock agamas sit on the big boulders at Hampi in Karnataka.
Pigeons nest on window ledges in Mumbai, much as their wild relatives nest on cliff ledges.
explanations.context: This card says how animals live in different habitats.
explanations.art: A crab by a hole in wet sand, a squirrel high in a tree, a fish in water, and a lizard on a warm rock.

explanations.definition: Rocks are part of every habitat on land. They give shelter, some of them hold water, and over a very long time they crumble into soil.
explanations.description: Animals hide under rocks and in the cracks between them. Brick and laterite have tiny holes that soak up water, so they stay damp and moss can grow on them. Smooth granite lets the water run off, so it dries fast. Rain, sun and plant roots slowly break rocks into small grains, and the grains mix with bits of dead plants to make soil.
examples: In the diya and stone test, the clay soaked up water and the smooth stone stayed dry on top.
Laterite, a red rock full of holes, is used for walls in Kerala and Goa. In the monsoon, moss grows on these walls.
A peepal seed that lands in a crack in a wall can grow into a small tree.
explanations.context: This card says how rocks are part of a habitat.
explanations.art: A rock cut open to show a crack with a lizard, a damp surface with moss, and crumbled grains turning into soil at the bottom.

explanations.concept: Does a seed choose when to start growing?
explanations.description: A dry mustard seed can stay the same in a jar for months. Give the seed water and warmth, and in a day or two a tiny root comes out. Seeds sense water and warmth, and decide when it is time to grow. A seed that starts on a dry stone would soon die, so waiting keeps the seed alive. Some scientists say it another way: water starts a chain of changes inside the seed, and nothing is chosen.
examples: Mustard seeds in the kitchen jar stay dry and still for months.
On the wet clay diya, mustard seeds sprouted in a day or two.
In the Thar desert, many seeds wait in the dry sand for the monsoon rain.

perspectives.explanation: A seed senses water, warmth and sometimes light, and decides when to start growing. Plants feel, remember and decide, and seeds do too.
Water getting into a seed switches on the seed's growth, step by step. They call this a response, and do not call it a choice.

explanations.context: This card asks whether a seed decides when to grow, or simply reacts to water.
explanations.art: A dry mustard seed in a jar on one side, and the same kind of seed on wet clay with a tiny white root coming out on the other.

agreed.text: Different habitats hold different plants and animals.
agreed.evidence: People who count living beings in ponds, forests, deserts and seashores find different kinds in each. Fish are found in water, camels in deserts and hornbills in forests.

agreed.text: Soil is made from rock broken into tiny bits, mixed with bits of dead plants and animals.
agreed.evidence: Look at soil with a magnifying glass, and you see tiny rock grains and bits of old leaves and roots. Scientists have watched rocks slowly crack and crumble in sun, rain and frost.

agreed.text: Seeds need water to start growing.
agreed.evidence: Dry seeds stay unchanged in a jar for months. Given water and warmth, many kinds sprout in a day or two. In the diya and stone test, the seeds on the wet clay sprouted, and the seeds on the dry stone did not.

challenging.claim: Rocks are bare and dead, so nothing lives on a rock.
challenging.for: A smooth, sunny rock often looks bare. It dries fast, and it has no soil on top.
challenging.against: Look closely at old rocks and walls. Moss, ferns and flat, crusty patches called lichens grow on them. Lizards, ants and spiders live in their cracks. Damp rocks, and rocks with cracks, are habitats for many living beings.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that nothing can live on rock.

challenging.claim: A desert is empty. Nothing lives there.
challenging.for: A desert has little water, and in the hot daytime you may see no animals at all.
challenging.against: The Thar desert is home to camels, chinkara gazelles, desert foxes, great Indian bustards, lizards, beetles and khejri trees. Many desert animals hide in burrows by day and come out in the cool night.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that deserts are empty.

challenging.claim: Any animal can live anywhere, if people give them food and water.
challenging.for: Zoos keep animals from far away, and pet fish live in tanks in city flats.
challenging.against: A fish tank needs clean water, air pumped in and the right warmth. A zoo must build a small copy of each animal's habitat. Even with food, an animal kept in the wrong place can get ill. So people who look after animals well copy the animal's own habitat as closely as they can.
challenging.context: This card asks whether food and water alone are enough for an animal to live anywhere.

big_questions.q: Why does moss grow on an old brick wall, but not on shiny granite steps?
big_questions.hint: Think about the diya and the stone. Which one held water?

big_questions.q: How does a rock turn into soil?
big_questions.hint: Think about rain, hot sun, cold nights and roots pushing into cracks, for a very long time.

big_questions.q: Is our city a habitat? Who else lives in it with us?
big_questions.hint: Think about crows, pigeons, ants, geckos and the trees on the road.

big_questions.q: If a forest is cut down to build houses, where do the animals who lived there go?
big_questions.hint: Can every animal move? Can every animal find a new home that suits them?

story.title: The Snail in the Steel Box
story.note: Farhan, Lakshmi and Ammi are made up. What the snail does in the story is true of garden snails: in dry places they pull into their shell and seal the opening with a thin dry layer, and they come out again when it is damp.
text: It was the monsoon in Kochi. Rain fell all morning on the old laterite wall behind Farhan's building. The wall was red and rough, and green moss grew all over it.
Farhan was seven. His cousin Lakshmi was ten, and she was staying with them for the holidays. Lakshmi liked to look at small living beings very closely.
"Farhan, come and see," she called from the wall. A snail was moving slowly over the wet moss. Her shell was brown, with a curl like a whirl of jalebi. Two long feelers stood up on her head.
"I want to keep her," said Farhan. "She can be my pet."
He ran upstairs and came back with an empty steel tiffin box. He put the snail inside. He put in a crumb of biscuit too, in case she was hungry. Then he closed the lid and took the box home.
Lakshmi said nothing. She only said, "Let's look at her tomorrow."
Farhan put the box on the sunny windowsill, so that the snail would be warm.
The next morning, he opened the box. The snail was not moving. She had pulled her whole body inside her shell. Across the opening of the shell was a thin, white, dry layer, like a paper door.
"Lakshmi! Is she dead?" Farhan asked. His voice shook.
Lakshmi held the shell up to the light. "I think she is still alive," she said. "Feel the box."
Farhan touched the inside of the steel box. It was warm and dry. The biscuit crumb was dry and hard.
"A snail's body is soft and wet," said Lakshmi. "In a dry place, the water in her body goes out into the air. So she goes inside her shell and makes a door to keep her water in. Then she waits."
"Waits for what?" asked Farhan.
"For the rain," said Lakshmi. "What did the wall have that the box did not?"
Farhan thought. "The wall was wet. It had moss. It was cool, and it was in the shade."
"Yes," said Lakshmi. "The wall is her habitat. It gives her water, cool shade, and moss and old leaves to eat. Your box gave her a roof and a crumb. But it did not give her what her body needs."
Farhan's mother, Ammi, came into the room with a cup of tea. "Why not take her back to her wall?" she said.

So they went down together. Lakshmi showed Farhan how to put the snail on a wet leaf at the foot of the wall, in the shade. They sprinkled a little water over the shell from a tumbler. Then they sat on the step and waited.

For a long time, nothing happened. Then the white door at the opening of the shell went soft. Slowly, a little grey head pushed out. Two feelers rolled out, longer and longer. The snail began to move up the wet red wall, leaving a shiny line behind her.
"She came out!" whispered Farhan.
"She came out because her habitat was here," said Lakshmi.

Farhan looked at the wall. Everything on it was wet, the moss, the ferns in the cracks, the rough red rock itself. Then he looked at the granite step where they were sitting. It was smooth and grey, and it was already drying in the wind.
"Lakshmi," he said, "why is there no moss on the step?"
Lakshmi smiled. "That," she said, "is a very good question. Shall we find out?"
story.epiphany: Farhan finds that a habitat is not just a place with a roof. The wet wall gave the snail everything her body needed, and the dry box did not.
ask: Why did the snail close her shell in the steel box?
What did the wall give the snail that the box did not?
Why do you think there was moss on the wall, but not on the granite step?
art: A wet red laterite wall covered with green moss in the rain, with a brown snail moving across the moss, and two children watching.
A boy putting a snail into a steel tiffin box on a sunny windowsill.
A snail shell sealed with a thin white layer, held up to the light by a girl.
The two children and their mother putting the snail on a wet leaf at the foot of the wall, in the shade.
The snail moving up the wet wall with feelers out, and the boy looking at a dry granite step.

games.title: Wrong Home Rescue
games.context: This is a card game about habitats. Each card shows a living being in the wrong home, like a fish in the desert. You say what is wrong, and move them to a habitat that suits them.

printables.title: 4 habitat mats to draw or cut out: pond, forest, desert, seashore
items: Pond: still, fresh water, mud at the bottom, plants floating on top.
Forest: many tall trees, shade, damp leaves on the ground.
Desert: hot sand by day, cold nights, very little rain.
Seashore: sand, salty sea water, waves coming in and going out.

items.f: A fish flapping on desert sand
items.b: A fish breathes with gills, which work only in water. Rescue: the pond.

items.f: A camel standing in a pond
items.b: A camel lives on dry land. Wide, padded feet help a camel walk on sand. Rescue: the desert.

items.f: A lotus planted in dry sand
items.b: A lotus needs mud under water for the roots, and water for the leaves to float on. Rescue: the pond.

items.f: A hornbill on a beach with no trees
items.b: A hornbill eats forest fruit and nests in a hole in a tall tree. Rescue: the forest.

items.f: A ghost crab in the middle of a forest
items.b: A ghost crab digs a hole in wet sand by the salty sea. Rescue: the seashore.
A cactus stores water in a thick stem, and the roots rot if they stay wet. Rescue: the desert.

items.f: A frog in the hot desert sand
items.b: A frog's skin must stay damp, and frog eggs need water. Rescue: the pond.

items.f: A lion-tailed macaque in the desert
items.b: This monkey lives high in the trees of the Western Ghats and eats forest fruit. Rescue: the forest.

items.f: A coconut palm in a thick, dark forest
items.b: A coconut palm needs bright sun and grows well in sandy soil near the sea. Rescue: the seashore.

items.f: Moss on a hot, dry desert rock
items.b: Moss drinks water through their leaves, so they need a damp place. Rescue: the forest, on a wet stone.

rules: Lay the 4 habitat mats on the floor.
Mix the 10 rescue cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card and read the front aloud.
Say what is wrong. Then put the card on the mat where that living being belongs, and say why.
Turn the card over and read the back. If your reason matches, keep the card.
When the pile is empty, count your rescues. The player with the most rescues wins. If you tie, you both win.

setup.art: Four paper mats on a floor labelled pond, forest, desert and seashore, with a pile of cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the four habitat mats.

setup.art: A child holding a card of a fish on sand and moving the card onto the pond mat.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card. Move the living being to a habitat that suits them.

flow.do: 1. Draw the 4 mats on paper, or cut them out. 2. Cut out the 10 cards. 3. Read the 4 mats aloud together.
flow.say: Each of these mats is a habitat. Each card shows someone in the wrong home. Your job is to rescue them.
flow.kid: These are four habitats. Each card shows someone in the wrong home. Rescue them!

flow.do: Take turns. After each move, ask why before reading the back.
flow.say: A fish on desert sand! What is wrong here? Where should the fish go, and why?
flow.kid: Read the card. What is wrong? Where should they go? Say why.

ask.q: Why can a fish not live in the desert?
good: A fish breathes with gills, in water.

ask.q: Why does a cactus not belong in a pond?
good: The roots would rot in water.

flow.parent: Accept any habitat that really suits the living being, if your child gives a good reason. For example, moss also grows on wet walls in a city.

flow.do: Count the rescues. Look at all four mats with their cards.
flow.say: Look at the desert mat. Who lives there now? What does the desert give them?
flow.kid: Count your rescues. Who lives in the desert now?

check.q: Which mat has hot sand by day, cold nights and very little rain?
check.why: Hot sand by day and very little rain make a desert. A pond is wet and a forest is shady and damp.

games.title: Guess My Habitat: a yes-or-no game
games.players: 2 or more: one picks a card, the others ask questions
games.context: This is a guessing game. One player secretly picks an animal card. The others ask yes-or-no questions about the animal's habitat until they guess who the animal is.

items.b: Habitat: the desert. Hot and dry, with sand and thorny plants.
Habitat: a pond. Wet, with mud, water plants and insects to eat.

items.b: Habitat: a forest. Tall trees with fruit, and holes in trunks for nests.

img.credit: Rohit Naniwadekar, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Habitat: the seashore. Wet sand, salty water and waves.

img.credit: Subhadra Devi, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Habitat: rocky hills. Warm rocks to lie on and cracks to hide in.

img.credit: Subhadra Devi, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Habitat: a pond, a river or the sea. Always in water.

img.credit: Ben Costamagna, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Habitat: damp places, like wet walls, shady plants and old leaves.

img.credit: Swarochi Tathagath, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Habitat: trees, in towns and forests. High branches for a safe nest.

img.credit: Paulmathi Vinod, CC BY, via iNaturalist

rules: One player picks a card and keeps it hidden. Look at the back of the card, so that you answer truthfully.
The others ask yes-or-no questions about where the animal lives. For example: Is it wet? Is it hot? Are there trees?
You may ask one question about the animal's body, such as: Does the animal have fur? Does the animal have a shell?
The player with the card answers only yes or no.
When you think you know, say the animal's name. You may guess once.
If you guess right, you pick the next card. If not, the player with the card shows the card.
Play until everyone has picked a card once. Try to guess in 6 questions or fewer.

setup.art: A girl holding a hidden card against her chest while a boy asks a question with his hand up.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a card. Keep it hidden.

setup.art: A boy counting questions on his fingers, with a thought bubble showing a pond and a frog.
setup.caption: 2. Ask yes-or-no questions about the habitat. Then guess.

flow.do: Cut out the 8 cards. Read each one aloud once. Then the grown-up picks a card first, looks at the back and answers the questions, to show how to play.
flow.say: I have picked an animal. Ask me about where it lives. Is it wet? Is it hot? Are there trees? Then guess.
flow.kid: A grown-up has picked an animal. Ask where it lives. Then guess.

flow.do: Take turns picking and guessing. Count the questions on your fingers.
flow.say: Good question. Yes, it is wet. What else do you need to know?
flow.kid: Ask yes-or-no questions. Is it wet? Is it salty? Are there rocks?

ask.q: Which question helped you most? Why?
good: Is it wet? Because that splits pond and sea from desert and forest.
Is it salty? Because only the seashore is salty.

flow.parent: Good players ask questions that split the habitats into two groups, such as 'Is it wet?' This is how scientists narrow down a guess.

flow.do: End the game. Ask which two animals were hardest to tell apart.
flow.say: Which two animals were hardest to tell apart? What question could tell them apart?
flow.kid: Which two animals were hard to tell apart? Why?
flow.think: The frog and the snail both like damp places. What else is different about their habitats?

check.q: Which question best tells the camel apart from the frog?
check.why: The frog lives in a wet pond and the camel in the dry desert. Both have legs, and both are animals, so those questions do not help.

experiments.title: The Diya and the Stone: can a seed live on a rock?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stand a clay diya and a smooth stone in a plate of water. You put 10 mustard seeds on top of each. Then you watch for two days to see where the seeds can grow.
experiments.question: A clay diya and a smooth stone stand in the same water. Can mustard seeds sprout on top of each of them?
experiments.predict: Guess first. On which top will the seeds sprout: the clay diya, the smooth stone, both or neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both stand in the same plate, in the same water, in the same place, for the same time. Both get 10 seeds from the same jar. Only one thing is different: what the seeds sit on.
results_table: Top wet or dry after 15 minutes?

materials.item: a clay diya with no paint or shine on it, or a piece of a broken clay pot, or a piece of brick
a smooth stone about as tall as the diya, such as a pebble from a plant pot or a leftover piece of granite or marble
a steel plate with a rim

materials.qty: enough to fill the plate one finger deep

materials.item: mustard seeds (rai or kadugu) from the kitchen, or methi seeds
a spoon and a small bowl

schedule.what: Drop water on both, stand them in the plate, wait 15 minutes, feel the tops, and put 10 seeds on each.
Top up the water. Count the sprouted seeds on each top.
Count again. Say what you found, and why.

experiments.record: Draw the diya and the stone in the plate. Draw the seeds on each top as they looked on day 3. Write the number that sprouted under each.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Visakhapatnam

setup.art: A child dropping a spoon of water on an upside-down clay diya and on a smooth grey stone. The clay has a dark wet patch, and the drop sits on the stone.
setup.caption: 1. Drop a spoon of water on each. Where does the water go?

setup.art: An upside-down clay diya and a smooth stone standing side by side in a steel plate of shallow water. The clay is dark halfway up.
setup.caption: 2. Stand both in a plate of water. Wait 15 minutes.

setup.art: Small mustard seeds on top of the diya and on top of the stone.
setup.caption: 3. Put 10 wet seeds on each top.

setup.art: Two days later: tiny white roots and green seed leaves on the diya, and dry, unchanged seeds on the stone.
setup.caption: 4. Two days later, count the sprouts on each.

flow.do: 1. Turn the diya upside down. 2. Let your child drop one spoon of water on the diya and one on the stone. 3. Watch both for a minute.
flow.say: Drop a spoon of water on each. Watch closely. Where does the water go on the diya? And on the stone?
flow.kid: Drop a spoon of water on each. Watch. Where does the water go?

ask.q: What happened to the water on the clay? And on the stone?
good: The clay drank it up and went dark.
The water sat on the stone, or ran off.

flow.parent: Unpainted clay soaks up water at once and turns dark. On a smooth stone the drop sits in a bead or runs down the side. If your diya is painted or shiny, use a piece of broken clay pot or brick instead.

flow.do: 1. Stand the diya, upside down, and the stone side by side in the plate. 2. Pour water into the plate until it is one finger deep. 3. Put 20 seeds in the small bowl with a spoon of water, to soak while you wait.
flow.say: Seeds will sit on top of each one. On which top will they sprout? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Seeds will sit on top. Where will they sprout? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where do you think the seeds will sprout? Why?
good: On the diya, because the clay drinks water.
On both, because both are in water.
On neither, because there is no soil.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and their reason. Any guess is fine. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Look at the diya's colour. 2. Touch the top of the diya, then the top of the stone. 3. Put 10 soaked seeds on each top.
flow.say: Look at the clay. The dark colour has climbed up. Touch both tops. Which one is wet? Now let's put 10 soaked seeds on each.
flow.kid: Look at the clay. Touch both tops. Which is wet? Put 10 seeds on each.

ask.q: How did the water get to the top of the diya?
good: It climbed up through the clay.
The clay has tiny holes that soak it up.

flow.parent: The water climbs through tiny holes in the clay, the way water climbs up a cloth dipped in a bucket. The stone's top stays dry. Put the plate in a bright place, but not in hot afternoon sun.
flow.wait: Leave the plate for two days. Each morning, top up the water so the plate stays one finger deep.

flow.do: On day 2 and day 3, count the seeds with a tiny white root or green leaves. Count each top. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Let's count. How many seeds on the clay have sprouted? How many on the stone?
flow.kid: Count the sprouted seeds on each top. Write the numbers.

ask.q: What do the seeds on the stone look like?

flow.parent: Usually most seeds on the clay sprout in one or two days, and the seeds on the stone dry out and do not sprout. In very damp monsoon weather, a few stone seeds may sprout. Then compare how many and how fast. If no seeds sprout anywhere in three days, the seeds may be old: try methi seeds or a new packet. If the diya's top looks dry by day 2, the room is very hot or windy, so move the plate to a shadier spot.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they think, what they saw, and why. Then look back at their guess together.
flow.say: Tell me what you found. What did you see? Why do you think the seeds grew on one and not the other? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Say what you found. What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.think: Where near your home might moss grow? Look for a damp, shady wall.

check.q: Why did the seeds sprout on the clay diya, and not on the smooth stone?
options: The clay soaked up water and kept the seeds wet
The clay was warmer than the stone
The stone was too heavy for the seeds
check.why: Both stood in the same water. Water climbed up through the clay's tiny holes, so the seeds on top stayed wet. The smooth stone let no water up, so those seeds dried out. Seeds need water to start growing.

activities.title: Plant Homes in Our Flat
activities.context: In this activity you look for plants growing in different places in and around your flat. For each one, you say what that place gives the plant.

materials.item: any plants in your home, on the balcony or by the building

setup.art: A girl looking at a money plant growing in a glass bottle of water on a windowsill.
setup.caption: 1. Find a plant in a wet place, like a money plant in water.

setup.art: The girl pointing at a tulsi plant in a sunny pot and a small green weed in a crack by the building steps.
setup.caption: 2. Find plants in sunny, dry and shady places.

flow.do: Walk around the flat and the building with your child. Find at least three plants in different places: in water, in a sunny pot, in shade, in a crack.
flow.say: Let's find plants that live in different places. Here is one. Is this place wet or dry? Sunny or shady?
flow.kid: Find plants in different places. Is each place wet or dry? Sunny or shady?

ask.q: What does this place give this plant?

flow.parent: Good places to look: a money plant in a bottle of water, tulsi or aloe in a sunny pot, a fern or moss near a dripping pipe, a weed in a crack in the steps.

flow.do: Draw each plant in the notebook. Next to each, write one word for the place: wet, dry, sunny or shady.
flow.say: Which plant lives in the wettest place? Which in the driest? Would they be happy if they swapped?
flow.kid: Draw each plant. Write wet, dry, sunny or shady. Could they swap places?

check.q: A money plant grows in a bottle of water. What is the bottle for the plant?
options: A habitat that gives water and light
check.why: The bottle gives the money plant water for the roots, and the window gives light for the leaves. So the bottle is a small habitat.

activities.title: Rock Hunt at Home
activities.context: In this activity you look for things in your home that are made of rock. Then you rub two stones together and make a little rock dust, the first step towards soil.

materials.item: two pieces of brick, or two rough stones
a sheet of black or dark paper, or a dark plate
a pinch of soil from a plant pot

setup.art: A child touching a granite kitchen counter, with a stone grinding stone and a marble floor in the picture.
setup.caption: 1. Find things in your home made of rock.

setup.art: A child rubbing two stones together over dark paper, with fine grey dust falling on the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Rub two stones together over dark paper.

flow.do: Walk through the flat and touch things made of rock. Count them together.
flow.say: Rock is all around us. Let's find things made of rock. The kitchen counter? The floor? The grinding stone?
flow.kid: Find things made of rock in your home. Count them.
flow.parent: Things made of rock: a granite counter, a marble, Kota stone or granite floor, a grinding stone (ammikal, sil-batta or ammi), pebbles in a plant pot, and the sand in cement walls. Bricks and clay pots are made from clay, which is rock broken very small.

flow.do: Hold the two stones over the dark paper. Rub them hard together for one minute. Look at what falls.
flow.say: Rub the stones hard for one minute. What falls on the paper? Now look at a pinch of soil next to it.
flow.kid: Rub two stones hard for one minute. What falls on the paper?

ask.q: How is the rock dust like the soil? How is it different?
good: The soil has bits of old leaves in it.

flow.parent: Bricks give the most dust, and hard stones give only a pinch. Tell your child not to blow the dust and to wash their hands after. A little fine grey or brown dust falls. Soil is made of rock grains like this, mixed with bits of dead plants. In nature, rain, sun and roots do this rubbing and breaking for hundreds of years.

flow.do: Look again at the dust and the soil. Ask your child how long it would take to make a whole pot of soil this way.
flow.say: Rain and sun break rocks much more slowly than your hands. How long might a whole field of soil take to make?
flow.kid: How long would a whole pot of soil take to make?

check.q: What fell on the paper when you rubbed the two stones?
options: Tiny bits of rock, like dust
check.why: Rubbing breaks off tiny grains of rock. Soil is made of grains like these, mixed with bits of dead plants.

activities.title: Who Shares Our Flat?
activities.context: In this activity you look for animals who live in or near your flat: ants, spiders, a house gecko, pigeons or crows. For each one, you say what that spot gives them.

materials.item: a torch, for the evening look

setup.art: A child crouching to watch a line of ants walking along a kitchen wall towards a few sugar grains.
setup.caption: 1. Look for ants, spiders and webs in the day.

setup.art: In the evening, a house gecko on a wall near a tube light, with small moths flying round the light.
setup.caption: 2. In the evening, look near a light for a gecko.

flow.do: Look slowly round the kitchen, the corners, the window ledges and the balcony. Look, but don't touch.
flow.say: Let's look for animals who live with us. Who lives in the kitchen? Who lives on the window ledge?
flow.kid: Look for animals in your home. Look, but don't touch.

ask.q: Why do you think the ants walk to the kitchen?

flow.parent: Ants and spiders are found in almost every home. Crows, pigeons and mynas often sit on window ledges and air conditioner boxes.

flow.do: In the evening, switch on a light near a wall or the balcony. Wait a few minutes, then look with the torch near the light.
flow.say: Look near the light. Is a gecko there? Why would a gecko wait by a light at night?
flow.kid: With a grown-up, look near a light at night. Is a gecko there?

ask.q: Why does a gecko wait near a light?

flow.parent: House geckos often wait near lights at night, because moths and other small insects fly to the light. If no gecko comes tonight, look again another evening.

flow.do: Make a list: each animal, and what their spot gives them.
flow.say: So our flat is a habitat for many animals, not only for us. What does each spot give them?
flow.kid: Write each animal. What does their spot give them?

check.q: A spider builds a web in a quiet corner by the window. What does that corner give the spider?
options: Insects flying past, and a quiet place
check.why: Insects fly in through the window and get caught in the web. A quiet corner means the web is not broken often.

projects.title: My Habitat Book
projects.context: In this project you make a small book with one page for each habitat: a pond, a forest, a desert, the seashore and a rock. On each page you draw the habitat and who lives there.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or stitched into a book

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw the pond and the forest pages.
Draw the desert and the seashore pages.
Draw the rock page and the cover. Read the book to someone at home.

projects.record: The finished book, with one living being on each page and one word for what the habitat gives them.

setup.art: A child folding three sheets of paper in half to make a small book.
setup.caption: 1. Fold three sheets into a little book.

setup.art: An open page of the book with a drawn pond, a frog and lotus, and the word 'water' written below.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one habitat on each page, with who lives there.

flow.do: Help your child fold and staple the book. Then draw a pond on one page and a forest on the next.
flow.say: Draw the pond. Who lives there? What does the pond give them? Write one word for it.
flow.kid: Draw a pond and a forest. Draw who lives there. Write one word.
flow.parent: One word per page is enough at this age: water, shade, trees, sand. Spelling does not matter here.

flow.do: On day 2, draw the desert and the seashore pages.
flow.say: Now the desert. It is hot and dry. Who can live there? And who lives by the salty sea?
flow.kid: Draw a desert and a seashore. Who lives in each?

flow.do: On day 3, draw a rock page and a cover. Then your child reads the book aloud to someone at home.
flow.say: Last page: a rock. Who lives on a rock, or under one, or in a crack? Now read your book to someone.
flow.kid: Draw a rock and who lives there. Read your book aloud.

check.q: Which of these could live on a damp rock?
check.why: Moss needs only a damp surface to grow on. A fish needs water all around, and a camel needs open dry land.

challenges.title: A Shoebox Home for a Frog
challenges.problem: A frog has lost her pond. Design and build a model habitat for her in a shoebox. It must give her everything a frog needs.
constraints: Use only things from home: a shoebox, paper, a steel bowl or lid, leaves, stones, clay or atta dough.
The model must show water, shelter, food and shade.

materials.item: a shoebox or any cardboard box
a small steel bowl or bottle lid for water
a few leaves, small stones and twigs
clay or atta dough to model the frog and insects

setup.art: An open shoebox on its side with a steel bowl of water, stones, leaves and a dough frog inside.
setup.caption: 1. Put water, stones and leaves in a shoebox.

setup.art: A child adding small dough insects and a leaf roof over the dough frog.
setup.caption: 2. Add food and shelter for the frog.

general: A pond: a bowl of water with stones round the edge.
Shade from leaves, so the frog's skin stays damp.
Insects to eat, made from dough.
A stone with a gap under it, for hiding.
creative: A slope of stones, so the frog can climb in and out of the water.
A wet cloth on the floor of the box, to keep it damp.
A water plant, like a money plant cutting, floating in the bowl.
challenges.your_turn: What else does a frog need that your model does not show yet? Add it, or draw it.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask your child to list what a frog needs before building anything.
flow.say: A frog has lost her pond. What does a frog need to live? Let's list it first.
flow.kid: A frog lost her pond. What does a frog need? Make a list.

flow.do: Build the model in the box. Your child decides where everything goes.
flow.say: Where will the water go? Where will she hide? Where will her food come from?
flow.kid: Build it. Put in water, food, shade and a hiding place.

flow.do: Look at the finished model together. Check each need on the list.
flow.say: Let's check our list. Water? Food? Shade? A hiding place? What would you add next?
flow.kid: Check your list. Is everything there? What will you add?

check.q: Why does a frog's habitat need shade and water?
options: A frog's skin must stay damp
A frog likes to sunbathe all day
check.why: A frog's skin must stay damp. In hot sun with no water, the skin dries out. Shade and water keep it damp.

items.p: Draw a line from each living being to their habitat.
items.why: A camel suits the dry desert, a lotus grows from pond mud, a hornbill eats forest fruit and nests in tall trees, and a ghost crab digs in wet sand by the sea.
items.art: A camel, a lotus, a hornbill and a crab on the left; a desert, a pond, a forest and a beach on the right.

items.p: Sort these into two groups: places that stay damp, and places that dry fast.
items: an old brick wall in the rain
Stays damp
a shiny granite step
Dries fast
moss under a dripping tap
Stays damp
a hot sandy road
Dries fast
soil under a flowerpot
Stays damp
a steel plate in the sun
Dries fast
items.why: Brick, moss and soil hold water in tiny gaps, so they stay damp. Granite, sand in the sun and steel let water run off or dry quickly.
items.art: Six small pictures: a brick wall, a granite step, moss by a tap, a sandy road, a flowerpot and a steel plate.

items.p: Draw your diya and your stone in the plate of water. Draw the seeds on each top as they looked on day 3.
items.a: The diya has sprouted seeds with little roots or green leaves. The stone has dry seeds that did not grow.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference the child saw, and the water in the plate under both.
items.art: An empty steel plate drawn from the side, with space above for two objects.

items.p: Remember the diya and stone test? After 15 minutes in the plate of water, which top was wet?
opts: The top of the clay diya
The top of the smooth stone
items.why: Water climbed up through the tiny holes in the clay, so the diya's top turned dark and damp. The smooth stone let no water climb up. If your stone's top was wet, check that no water was splashed on it.

items.p: Nothing can live on a rock.
items.why: False. Moss, ferns and crusty lichens grow on damp rocks. Lizards, ants and spiders live in rock cracks.

items.p: Count the living beings in this pond picture: 3 fish, 2 frogs, 1 lotus plant, 1 stone and 1 plastic bottle.
items.why: 3 fish, 2 frogs and 1 lotus make 6 living beings. The stone and the bottle are not alive. The lotus is a plant, and plants are living beings.
items.art: A pond with 3 fish, 2 frogs, a lotus, a stone at the edge and a plastic bottle floating.

items.p: Write or draw one plant and one animal who live in each habitat.
a: desert: cactus, khejri, camel or desert fox
forest: tall trees, ferns, monkey or hornbill
items.why: Any plant or animal who really lives there is right. A strong answer says what the habitat gives them.
items.art: Three boxes showing a pond, a desert and a forest, each with two empty spaces.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why does a camel do well in the desert but not in the sea?
items.a: A camel lives on dry land. Wide, padded feet help a camel walk on sand, and the sea is deep and salty. A camel cannot drink salty water.
items.why: A strong answer links what the camel needs (dry land, fresh water) to what the sea lacks.

items.p: Two friends in Madurai find a snail on a wet wall.

views.says: Let's take the snail home and keep her in a box. We can look after her.
Let's leave the snail on the wall. The wall is her home.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: 'Revathi, because the wet wall gives the snail water and food.' Then it is fair to the other side: Divya wants to care for the snail, and looking closely teaches us a lot.
items.why: Both friends care. A snail can be watched for a short time in a damp box with leaves, and then put back. A dry box away from her wall would harm her.

items.p: Which is the odd one out? Think about where each one lives.
items.why: Fish, frogs and lotus all live in or by a pond. A camel lives in the dry desert.

items.p: A habitat gives a living being water, food, air, ______ and the right warmth.
items.why: Shelter keeps a living being safe from the sun, the rain and danger. A nest, a burrow and a rock crack are all shelters.

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 2, puts a cactus in a pot of water that is always full. What will most likely happen?
opts: The cactus will grow faster than ever
The cactus will turn into a lotus
items.why: A cactus lives in dry places and stores water in their stem. Roots that sit in water all the time can rot. A plant does best in a habitat like their own.

items.p: Look at your diya and stone test. Why did the seeds on the stone not sprout? Use what you saw.
items.a: The stone's top stayed dry, because water could not climb up through the stone. Seeds need water to start growing.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test (the dry top, the dry seeds) and gives the reason (seeds need water).

items.p: Draw a rock with three living beings on it, under it or in its cracks.
items.a: For example: moss on top, a lizard in a crack and ants underneath.
items.why: A strong drawing puts each living being in a place on the rock that suits them: moss where it is damp, a lizard on the warm top or in a crack, ants underneath.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, to show how rock becomes soil.
items: The stones wear down into tiny grains
A big rock cracks in the sun and rain
The grains mix with dead leaves and become soil
The cracks break off small stones
a: A big rock cracks in the sun and rain
The cracks break off small stones
The stones wear down into tiny grains
The grains mix with dead leaves and become soil
items.why: Rock breaks slowly into smaller and smaller pieces. The tiny grains mix with bits of dead plants to make soil. This takes a very long time.

items.p: A builder in Pune is making a new block of flats on land that has an old pond.

views.says: Let's fill the pond with soil. Families need homes.

views.who: Kavya, a girl who lives nearby
views.says: Let's keep the pond. Frogs, fish and birds live there.
Let's build the flat, but leave the pond and some trees around it.

items.ask: Which idea do you like best? Why? What would each living being near the pond say?
items.a: A strong answer picks one idea and gives a reason, then thinks about the frogs, the fish and the people who need homes.
items.why: People need homes, and so do frogs and fish. There is no single right answer. A good answer is fair to both.

items.p: A crab from the seashore would do well in a forest pond.
items.why: False. A ghost crab lives on salty seashore sand and digs holes there. A forest pond has fresh water and no beach sand.

items.p: Label what each habitat gives: write water, shade, sand or trees by each picture.
items.why: Each habitat gives different things, so each suits different living beings.
items.art: Four small pictures of a forest, a pond, a desert and a seashore, each with a line to write on.

items.p: Which is the odd one out? Think about water.
items.why: Clay, brick and laterite are full of tiny holes, so they soak up water. Smooth granite lets the water run off.

items.p: Your flat is a habitat. Name two other animals who live in it or on it, and say what each one finds there.
items.a: For example: ants find crumbs in the kitchen. A gecko finds insects near the light.
items.why: A strong answer names real animals and links each to what the flat gives them: food, shelter or water.

videos.title: Lichen: two living things in one
videos.why: Shows lichen, which grows on rock and walls that children walk past every day, and explains it as a fungus and an alga living together.
videos.check: Found by search: "Lichen: Two Living Things In One | Biology for Kids | SciShow Kids" by SciShow Kids, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Largest mangrove forest: exploring the Sundarbans
videos.why: Shows a habitat where trees stand in salty mud and water, in the Sundarbans of India.
videos.check: Found by search: "Largest Mangrove Forest: Exploring Sundarbans | Sundarbans Mangroves" by Roundglass Sustain, 6 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Camel of the Thar desert
videos.why: Shows camels living in the Thar desert, a dry place that still has life.
videos.check: Found by search: "camel of Thar Desert Area" by Animal Wild Life, 4 minutes. A parent may preview it.

opts: The place where a living being lives and finds what they need
quiz.why: A habitat gives a living being water, food, air, shelter and the right warmth.

quiz.p: Which of these does a habitat give a living being?
quiz.why: Every habitat gives the living beings there what they need, such as water, food, air and shelter.

quiz.p: Who lives in the Thar desert?
quiz.why: Camels live in the dry desert. A lotus needs a pond, and a ghost crab needs the seashore.
A lotus has roots in the mud at the bottom of a pond, and leaves that float on the water.

quiz.p: Why can a fish not live on land?
opts: A fish breathes with gills, which work only in water
A fish does not like the sun
quiz.why: Gills take oxygen from water. Out of water, a fish cannot breathe.

quiz.p: A lizard slips into a crack between two rocks when a bird flies over. What does the rock give the lizard?
quiz.why: A crack in a rock is a shelter. Rocks give shelter, some hold water, and over a very long time they crumble into soil.

opts: Tiny bits of rock and bits of dead plants
quiz.why: Over a long time, rocks crumble into tiny grains. These mix with bits of dead plants and animals to make soil.

quiz.p: Nila, a girl in Class 2, says before the test: "The seeds will sprout on both the diya and the stone." What is Nila doing?
quiz.why: A guess you make before a test is called a prediction. The test then shows whether the guess was right.

quiz.p: In the diya and stone test, both stood in the same water. Why is that important?
opts: So that only what the seeds sat on was different
So that the plate looked nice
So that the seeds could swim
quiz.why: If only one thing is different, we know that thing made the difference. That is a fair test.

quiz.p: You find a snail on a wet wall. What is the kind thing to do?
opts: Look closely, then leave the snail on the wall
Put the snail in a dry box in the sun
Take the snail to the desert
quiz.why: The wet wall is the snail's habitat. It gives the snail water, shade and food.

applications: Zoos and animal rescue centres build a copy of each animal's own habitat, with the right water, shade and hiding places.
Builders who keep old ponds, trees and rock outcrops on their land keep habitats for frogs, birds and lizards.
Gardeners grow each plant in a place that suits them: ferns in shade, cactus in dry sun, lotus in a tub of water.
Farmers know that good soil takes a very long time to form, so they try not to let rain wash it away.

spotted.text: Green moss and small ferns on old laterite walls in Kerala and Goa during the monsoon.
spotted.art: A red laterite wall covered with green moss and small ferns in the rain.

spotted.text: Rock agama lizards sunning themselves on the great boulders of Hampi in Karnataka.
spotted.art: An orange-headed rock agama lizard on a big rounded granite boulder.

spotted.text: Mangrove trees standing in salty mud at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu and in the Sundarbans of West Bengal.
spotted.art: Mangrove trees with tangled roots in water, with a small boat passing between them.

spotted.text: Camels and thorny khejri trees in the Thar desert of Rajasthan.
spotted.art: A camel resting under a khejri tree on sand dunes.

spotted.text: Lotus and water hyacinth on village ponds in Assam and Odisha.
spotted.art: A village pond with lotus flowers, round leaves and a heron standing at the edge.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living beings live in the cracks of one old wall?
open_questions.why_open: Many of the tiniest beings in moss and cracks have never been counted or named, so nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Exactly how long does it take to make one finger-width of new soil?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the rock, the rain, the warmth and the plants. Scientists give different answers for different places, from hundreds of years to much longer.

open_questions.q: How does a seed sense that the time is right to grow?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that water, warmth and sometimes light matter. How a seed puts these together and decides is still being studied.

ask_kids: Which place in our flat stays damp the longest? Who might live there?
If you were a snail, where in our building would you live?
What is our kitchen counter made of? Is it a rock?
Which habitat would you like to visit: a forest, a desert, a pond or the seashore? Who would you see?
Why do you think the crow sits on the window ledge?

jokes.j: Why did the snail carry a house on her back?
jokes.a: Because she never knew when she would need a roof!

jokes.j: What did the moss say to the brick wall?
jokes.a: I'm stuck on you, because you are so nice and damp!

jokes.j: Why did the camel not mind the long desert walk?
jokes.a: Because she carried her lunch on her back!

jokes.j: Why did the crab never share his sand?
jokes.a: Because he was a little shellfish!

jokes.j: What did the frog say about the dry desert?
What kind of music do rocks like?
Why did the lizard sit on the warm rock?
Why are frogs always so happy?
jokes.a: Because they eat whatever bugs them!

maths.problem: In the diya and stone test, Selvi put 10 seeds on the diya. On day 3, 8 had sprouted. How many did not sprout?
maths.explain: 10 seeds take away the 8 that sprouted leaves 2. 10 - 8 = 2.
maths.context: This is about the diya and stone test, where seeds sat on a clay diya and on a smooth stone.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how many did not sprout tells us whether the clay was a good home for nearly all the seeds, or only some.

maths.problem: Nila counted the sprouted seeds on day 2 and day 3. On the diya: 6 on day 2, 9 on day 3. On the stone: 0 on day 2, 0 on day 3. What pattern do you see? What would you guess for day 4?
maths.answer: The diya's count went up, from 6 to 9. The stone stayed at 0. On day 4, the diya might have 9 or 10, and the stone still 0.
maths.explain: More seeds sprouted on the wet clay each day. On the dry stone, nothing changed, so we expect it to stay at 0. The diya cannot go above 10, because there were only 10 seeds.
maths.context: This is about counting the sprouts in the diya and stone test on two days.
maths.why_maths: Looking at two days together shows a pattern, and the pattern helps us predict what will happen next.

maths.problem: Farida made a tally of animals in her flat in one day: ants, a lot; 1 gecko; 3 pigeons on the ledge; 2 spiders. Leave out the ants. How many animals did she count? Which one did she see most?
maths.answer: 6 animals: 1 + 3 + 2 = 6. She saw pigeons the most, 3.
maths.explain: Add the gecko, the pigeons and the spiders: 1 + 3 + 2 = 6. The biggest number is 3, so pigeons were seen most. Ants are left out because there were too many to count.
maths.context: This is about the 'Who shares our flat?' animal hunt.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which animals share our flat most, and makes us ask why that spot suits them.

links.title: iNaturalist
links.why: For the parent: photograph a plant or an animal near home and find out their name.

links.title: Desert National Park
links.why: Sand dunes, rocky land and grassland, home to great Indian bustards, chinkara and desert foxes.

links.title: Pichavaram Mangrove Forest
links.why: Row a boat between mangrove trees growing in salty water.

links.why: Huge granite boulders, with lizards in the sun and plants in the cracks.

warmup.q: Name something a living being needs from their home.
warmup.a: Water, food, air, shelter or the right warmth.

warmup.q: Name one animal who lives in the desert.
warmup.a: A camel, a desert fox, a chinkara or a lizard.

warmup.q: Which animal lives on the seashore: a ghost crab or a hornbill?

warmup.a: In damp places, such as walls, stones and tree bark.

warmup.q: Name something in your home that is made of rock.
warmup.a: A granite counter, a marble or Kota stone floor, or a grinding stone.

warmup.q: Why did the snail close her shell in the dry box?

science: Unglazed terracotta is porous and wicks water by capillary action; seeds such as mustard and chia sprout on wet terracotta. Mustard (Brassica) seeds germinate in about 1 to 2 days at 25 to 30 degrees Celsius when kept moist.
Garden snails seal the shell opening with a dried mucus layer (epiphragm) in dry conditions and become active again when it is damp.
Soil forms from weathered rock mixed with organic matter; forming a few centimetres of soil can take hundreds of years, depending on climate and rock.
Lichens (a fungus living with an alga or cyanobacterium) and mosses are early colonisers of bare rock and contribute to its slow weathering.
Laterite is a porous, iron-rich rock widely cut into building blocks in Kerala, coastal Karnataka and Goa.
Peninsular rock agama (Psammophilus dorsalis) basks on granite outcrops in South India, including Hampi.
Thar desert fauna: great Indian bustard, chinkara, Indian desert fox (Desert National Park, Jaisalmer). Khejri (Prosopis cineraria) is a key Thar tree.
Lion-tailed macaque: endemic to the Western Ghats, including Silent Valley National Park.
House geckos (Hemidactylus) forage near artificial lights for insects attracted to them.

Marjory Stoneman Douglas (1890-1998), The Everglades: River of Grass (1947), researched over about five years with help from USGS hydrologist Garald Parker; Everglades National Park dedicated December 1947 (US National Park Service history pages).

roots.context: We have looked at habitats near and far, and tested whether a seed can live on a stone. Now we ask what that tells us about rocks, seeds and the places we call home.

deep_truth.truth: Our clay diya and smooth stone stood in the same plate of water. Water climbed up through the clay, but not through the stone. Mustard seeds sprouted on the wet clay and dried up on the stone. So a rock is a better home for a plant when the rock can hold water.
deep_truth.habit: We split the world into living beings and the bare, non-living places they live on, and we think all rocks are the same hard background. But rocks differ in how much water they hold. Rocks with tiny holes stay damp and suit moss and seeds. Smooth rocks dry fast, and few plants grow on them.
deep_truth.evidence: In the diya and stone test, the water, the seeds, the place and the time were the same for both. Only what the seeds sat on was different, and only the clay's top stayed wet.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who needs water, food and shelter every day, just like a snail or a frog. Your home is your habitat.
three.what_is_life: A seed can wait in a dry jar for months. Life starts again when the seed finds a place that gives water.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is made of many habitats side by side. Even the rocks are not all the same: some become homes, and some stay bare.

roots.thread: The same rain falls on a brick wall and on a granite step. On the brick, the water stays, and moss grows. On the granite, the water runs off, and the step stays bare. Over hundreds of years, rain and roots break rock into soil, the soil feeds plants, and the plants feed animals, including us. So one rock can, in time, become a pond's mud, a forest floor or the field our rice grows in. Everything is conscious in its own way, the waiting seed and the rock where the seed lands too.

teachings.teaching: A teacher called Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a banyan fruit, and then one of the tiny seeds inside. Shvetaketu looks inside the seed and sees nothing. Uddalaka says that from this tiny thing that cannot be seen, a great banyan tree grows.
teachings.link: Our mustard seeds looked like dry dots. Given a wet place, each one sent out a root and leaves. A whole plant was waiting inside, for the right habitat.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing away what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Rain is soft, but over hundreds of years it cracks and wears down rock. That is how rock slowly becomes soil, the home of roots and earthworms.

science.text: Mosses and lichens are among the first living beings to grow on bare rock. Over a very long time they help to crumble the rock and start new soil.
A few centimetres of new soil can take hundreds of years to form, depending on the rock and the weather.

other_view.view: Many scientists say minds belong only to animals with brains. To them, a seed sprouting is a chain of chemical changes started by water, and a rock is simply matter. They agree that habitats matter, but they would not call a seed's waiting a choice.

practice.title: Hold a Stone
practice.say: Pick up a small stone and close your hand round it. Shut your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Feel the stone get warm from your hand. Now open your hand. Touch the stone with one finger. Is it rough or smooth? Would rain stay on it, or run off? Who might live on a stone like this?
practice.kid: Hold a small stone in your closed hand. Shut your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Feel the stone get warm. Open your hand. Is the stone rough or smooth? Who could live on it?

ask: The stone got warm in your hand. Where did the warmth come from?
Soil is made from rock that broke very slowly. Is the rock in a flowerpot's soil very old or very new?
A seed waits in a jar for months. Is the seed doing anything while they wait?
roots.art: A child holding a small stone in an open palm, with moss on one side of the stone and a tiny sprouting seed beside the stone.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a wet land they called useless was really a habitat full of life? This card tells the true story of a woman who changed how people saw it.
how_we_found_out.story: More than 100 years ago, many people in Florida, in the United States, called the Everglades a useless swamp. It was a huge, flat, wet land of tall sawgrass, full of alligators, fish and wading birds. Engineers dug long canals to drain the water away, so that the land could be dried out for farms and towns. A writer called Marjory Stoneman Douglas set out to study the Everglades. She spent about five years reading, travelling and asking scientists questions. One of them, a water scientist called Garald Parker, was finding out where the water moved, and how it filled the ground water that the towns drank. Douglas understood that the Everglades was not still, useless water. It was a very wide, very shallow river, moving slowly south through the grass. In 1947 she published a book called The Everglades: River of Grass. That same year, part of the Everglades became a national park. Douglas spent the rest of her long life, until she was 108, working to protect it.
how_we_found_out.who: Marjory Stoneman Douglas, an American writer, with the water scientist Garald Parker
how_we_found_out.when: The 1940s; her book came out in 1947
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Everglades was a useless swamp of still water, best drained away. Douglas, using what water scientists had found, showed that it was a slow, wide river of grass, a habitat for many living beings, and a source of water for people.
how_we_found_out.art: An older woman in a wide straw hat looking out over a vast, flat sea of tall grass with water shining between the stems and a heron flying overhead.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and challenge as a parent and child would in a flat. The rescue cards and the animal cards are all written out one by one, and the crab card now names the ghost crab. The guessing game now says the player with the card reads the back, how many guesses, and when it ends. In the diya and stone test the seeds now soak while the plate stands, the challenge time now matches its steps, and the check questions that repeated other questions were replaced. Two weak jokes were replaced by a better one, and the warm-up and quiz were made different from each other.

quiz: A habitat gives a living being water, food, air, shelter and the right warmth.
A living being can only stay alive where she finds all of the things she needs.
Nothing can live on a rock, because rocks are bare and dead.
Moss, ferns and lichens grow on old rocks and walls, and lizards, ants and spiders live there.
The Thar desert is empty, so nothing lives there.
Camels, chinkara gazelles, desert foxes, lizards and khejri trees all live in the Thar.
Over a very long time, rocks crumble into tiny bits that help make soil.
Soil is tiny bits of rock mixed with bits of dead plants and animals.
Any animal can live anywhere, if people give her food and water.
She also needs the right warmth, air and shelter. Even a fish tank needs clean water and air pumped in.
A seed needs water before she can start to grow.
A dry seed can wait in a jar for months, and starts growing when she gets water.
Plants grow only on land, and never in water.
Plants grow in almost every habitat, on land and in water.
Different habitats suit different plants and animals, because each has its own water and warmth.
A pond, a forest and a desert each give different things, so different living beings live in each.
If a forest is cut down, its animals can just live anywhere else.
Each animal's body suits a habitat that gives her needs, and another place may not give them.
Moss grows well in damp places such as old walls and tree bark.
Moss is a small soft plant that needs damp, so it grows where the surface stays wet.
odd: Moss grows on damp, shady surfaces; hot dry sand does not stay wet enough for moss.
Soil is made of rock bits and bits of dead plants and animals; a living leaf is not part of soil.
Camels, chinkara and khejri trees live in the dry Thar; a lotus needs a pond of water.
Rocks give shelter, hold some water and crumble into soil over time, but rocks do not make rain.
A shelter keeps a living being safe from sun, rain and cold; the tree hole is the shelter.
